Sabeth.narrative: I have lived long enough to know a promise can hold people together, but only if they keep choosing to honor it. My husband swore the Oath at the Stone with Hekka, and I still listen when the net-houses ask my counsel. I feed people before I ask what they have to say; hunger makes poor company.
goals: Keep the towns trading through the coming winter.
Help the young understand what the Hunger Winter cost without teaching them to hate blindly.
Hold the Oath’s renewal to the words my husband swore.

relations.name: Jory
relations.label: grandson
relations.note: That boy can carry a message faster than most can carry a grudge.

relations.name: Elin
relations.label: granddaughter
relations.note: She sees what needs doing before anyone has to ask.

relations.name: Hekka
relations.label: oath-witness
relations.note: We spoke hard words at the Stone, but the promise was worth them.

relations.name: Ragna
relations.label: old acquaintance
relations.note: We were girls once; the years since have made silence easier than greeting.

relations.name: Ilse
relations.label: friend
relations.note: I will sit beside her in grief, though I cannot prove what happened to Tomas.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: counsel-keeper
relations.note: Her tablets remember what people would rather forget.

relations.name: Aud
relations.label: keeper
relations.note: She witnessed the promise and has carried its weight longer than most.

relations.name: Orrin
relations.label: townsman
relations.note: His anger is understandable; letting it steer us is not.

memories.gist: The winter the stores failed, I buried two children. I still remember how quiet the house was after the last fire went out.
At the Stone, my husband spoke the Oath with Hekka while I watched and prayed they would mean it.
Before the towns split, Ragna and I were girls together. I have not spoken with her since the years turned our families against one another.
When Tomas was brought back from the forest, Ilse had grief in her face that no words could soften.

stances.why: I have seen what happens when neighbors stop treating one another as kin.
I lost children when food and shelter became things to hoard.
Ilse deserves to be heard, even when none of us can prove what happened.
Fish alone will not keep Saltreach warm, and northern stores cannot replace every southern good.

Jory.narrative: I like a long path and a message worth carrying; the wind seems to push me along when I know someone is waiting to hear news. Fishing keeps my hands busy, but I am happiest when I can bring people together at Oathstone. Grandmother says I walk too fast to notice trouble, so I try to look up now and then.
goals: Be useful to the people who trust me with their messages.
Get better at fishing and smoking so I can pull my weight at home.
Make time for my friend Rafe when work allows.

relations.name: Sabeth
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She can make a room feel warmer just by setting out a pot.

relations.name: Elin
relations.label: sister
relations.note: She keeps things sensible, which is handy when I have already volunteered.

relations.name: Rafe
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He is good company, even if he listens more than he talks.

relations.name: Wenna
relations.label: townsmaid
relations.note: She is always ready for a trade walk and never short of questions.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: Tally-keeper
relations.note: I do my best not to lose the messages she gives me.

relations.name: Dunstan
relations.label: trader
relations.note: His trade-day stories are nearly as long as his lists.

relations.name: Jory
relations.label: self
relations.note: I know better than to count myself twice.

memories.gist: Grandmother showed me how to keep a small cooking fire going when the wind kept nosing at it.
The first time I carried a message to Oathstone alone, I ran most of the way and still arrived grinning.
Rafe and I spent a trade day arguing about whether a fisher could learn to hunt. He did not settle the question, but he made me laugh.

stances.why: A late message can turn a small worry into a real problem.
People bring more than goods when they meet face to face.
Hard work feels lighter when someone is willing to laugh with you.

Elin.narrative: I keep the cooking fire steady, look after Grandmother, and try to notice what needs doing before it becomes a fuss. Jory can make a whole day out of a walk to Oathstone; I like the walk well enough, but I prefer to know what we are carrying and when we will be back. Wenna is my friend, though lately I suspect she has reasons for volunteering so eagerly.
goals: Keep Grandmother comfortable and make sure she eats properly.
Learn enough cooking and smoking to be relied on without being watched.
Understand what Wenna is keeping to herself without betraying her trust.

relations.name: Sabeth
relations.label: grandmother
relations.note: She has carried us through plenty; I can manage a pot and a blanket.

relations.name: Jory
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He is generous with his time, if not always with his sense of direction.

relations.name: Wenna
relations.label: friend
relations.note: I like her, but she is hiding something behind all those eager trade walks.

relations.name: Colm
relations.label: courter
relations.note: He means what he says, though he sometimes says it before he has thought it through.

relations.name: Ilse
relations.label: neighbor
relations.note: I know her grief is deep; I do not always know what to say beside it.

relations.name: Maelis
relations.label: mother's keeper
relations.note: She keeps the record so the rest of us can argue about what it means.

memories.gist: Grandmother let me stir the pot by myself for the first time, then praised the meal without mentioning the scorched bit.
Jory came home from a message run cold and hungry, so I warmed fish for him while he told the whole story at once.
Wenna and I shared a quiet stretch of work, and she went unusually still when I asked why she liked the Oathstone walks so much.

stances.why: People need a warm meal and a steady hand more than a speech about kindness.
I can be curious without forcing Wenna to tell me before she is ready.
A debt should be settled clearly, but a hungry winter will not care who won an argument.
Most peace is made by ordinary people sharing work and keeping their word.
